Spark Program | ServiceSeal: Prepaid Utility Passes on CKB, Piloted at a Charging Kiosk in Lagos
Applicant: Hardik Azmi (GitHub: DegenerateAlchemist (Yugi) · GitHub )
Funding requested: $900 USD
Timeline: 6 weeks
Category: CKB Application / Retail Utility & State Primitives
Repository: GitHub - DegenerateAlchemist/service-seal · GitHub
1. Summary
Where I stay in Lagos, Nigeria power is terrible so people rely on neighbourhood charging kiosks to keep their phones, lamps and power banks working. Regular customers usually pay upfront for a few charges instead of paying every single time they drop a phone off
I own one of these charging kiosks though I don’t run it myself daily, I have someone employed there handling customers while I’m away. Right now, prepaid balances are written down in a paper notebook at the shop. When a customer insists they paid for five charges and only used two, while the notebook says four, the customer has no way to verify the record on their own. Since I’m not sitting at the shop, I only hear about the argument after.
ServiceSeal moves that notebook record into a live CKB Cell. A customer gets a prepaid pass holding a set number of units. Each time they charge a device, my attendant logs the debit and the pass Cell updates to a new Cell with the lower balance and the next sequence number. A CKB Type Script checks that the sequence goes up by one, the balance drops by the exact amount recorded and the balance never drops below zero. Since a Cell can only be spent once, two conflicting updates can’t both go through. Both the customer and I can check the full usage history directly from CKB without relying on the notebook at the shop.
2. Team Profile
Applicant: Hardik Azmi (DegenerateAlchemist on GitHub)
Role: Full-stack and smart contract developer, and owner of the Lagos charging kiosk used for the pilot
Contact: Nervos Talk
Background: I built Stellar Kit, an open-source tool for building, deploying and simulating smart contracts on Stellar that was funded by Stellar WA. I have also built different solutions across Solana, Stellar/Soroban, Sui and EVM. On CKB, I have worked on a CKB script and built the initial TypeScript core for ServiceSeal (v0.1.0). I am new to Fiber and this proposal does not use it.
3. The Problem
Around here in Lagos, people buy most daily utilities in small retail portions: phone and battery charging, cooking gas refills, water and shared equipment time. Prepaid tabs are very common because customers like locking in credit when they have cash and shop owners want steady repeat customers.
When you own the shop but have an employee running the counter, three issues come up all the time:
Customer and attendant arguments: The customer has no proper receipt trail showing their starting balance and every deduction made from it.
Owner and attendant reconciliation: When I check in at the end of the day, I cannot tell from home if numbers in the notebook were changed, scratched out or skipped.
No simple tool for small retail utilities: Big companies can run custom backend databases, but for a local kiosk or gas shop, spinning up a standard database still leaves the exact same trust problem since the operator can edit rows whenever they want.
4. How It Works
Terms used in this proposal:
Pass Cell: A live CKB Cell holding one customer’s prepaid balance for a specific terminal.
Terminal: The signing key used at the kiosk to log usage.
Usage receipt: A signed message with the session ID, terminal ID, sequence number and units used.
Successor Cell: The new Pass Cell created when a usage receipt is applied.
Open pass. A pass is created on CKB testnet with a starting unit balance (like 100 units) and sequence = 0, tied to the kiosk’s terminal ID and key hash.
Record usage. When a customer charges a device, the terminal signs a receipt for the units used with sequence = last_sequence + 1. The transaction spends the old Pass Cell, puts the signed receipt in the witness and creates the Successor Cell with remaining_units = old_units - usage and sequence = old_sequence + 1.
Check history. Anyone with the pass ID can open the web page or run the CLI tool to pull every debit from CKB transaction history and check the remaining balance without calling a ServiceSeal server.
What it covers and what it doesn’t. Since my attendant is the one typing in the usage at the kiosk, a script on CKB obviously cannot stop someone from entering a wrong number in the first place. What it does is make sure that once a debit is recorded, it cannot be more than the customer’s remaining balance, cannot be replayed twice, cannot be quietly edited or erased later in the day and is visible right away to both the customer and me.
5. Technical Architecture
Already built (not funded by this grant):
The repository (v0.1.0) already has the off-chain protocol logic working in TypeScript:
Fixed 100-byte SS01 Cell data layout (session_id, terminal_id, device_key_hash, remaining_units and last_sequence).
Ed25519 receipt signing and verification.
Sequence and balance transition checks.
CKB witness encoding (encodeSessionWitness) and batch transitions (applyReceiptBatch).
14 rejection tests covering replay, altered usage, wrong terminal, wrong session, skipped sequence, overdraw and bad state formatting.
Funded by this grant:
ServiceSeal Type Script (CKB-VM): Enforces the SS01 transition rules on-chain:
session_id, terminal_id and device_key_hash stay the same between the input and output Pass Cells.
output.last_sequence == input.last_sequence + 1.
output.remaining_units == input.remaining_units - receipt.usage and receipt.usage > 0.
Terminal authorisation check. Week 1 validates this in CKB-VM first to measure cycle cost and cell capacity before building the rest of the app around it.
Transaction Builder & Verifier CLI: TypeScript functions using CCC to open a pass, send a debit transaction on Pudge testnet and rebuild a pass’s history straight from CKB RPC/indexer.
Kiosk Web UI (Testnet): A simple three-page web app (Open Pass, Kiosk Terminal and Pass History) that my attendant and regular customers will test during a two-week pilot at the kiosk alongside our usual paper notebook.
POC Scope:
Testnet only (Pudge), using test units alongside normal cash/transfer payments at the kiosk.
Out of scope for this grant: mainnet deployment, real money custody, Fiber channels, hardware meters or a formal security audit.
6. Deliverables
ServiceSeal Type Script: CKB-VM script checking the pass rules, deployed on Pudge testnet, with tests covering valid updates and invalid attempts (replay, skipped sequence, overdraw, wrong terminal, changed identity fields and bad cell data).
Transaction SDK & History Verifier: Open-source TypeScript module and CLI command that builds create and debit transactions with CCC and rebuilds any pass’s history from CKB testnet RPC without a backend.
Kiosk Testnet Web App: Simple browser UI for opening a pass, logging kiosk usage and checking pass history by ID, plus a short video showing the full flow and an overdraw transaction getting rejected on-chain.
Lagos Kiosk Pilot & Report: Two-week pilot run at my charging kiosk with my employee and regular customers, written up in a final post on Nervos Talk with testnet transaction hashes, cycle and capacity numbers and honest notes on how it went.
All code will be open-source under the MIT license.
7. Roadmap
Milestone
Timeline
Work
1. On-chain check & script layout
Week 1
Test SS01 witness and authorisation checks in CKB-VM, measure cycle cost and cell capacity and post the Week 1 numbers. If the signature check costs too many cycles, switch to a simpler terminal lock-check before moving on.
2. Core Type Script & rejection tests
Weeks 2 to 3
Write the full Type Script and rejection test suite (replay, overdraw, skipped sequence, wrong terminal/session and bad output size) and deploy to Pudge testnet.
3. CCC transaction builder & Web UI
Week 4
Hook up CCC transaction building to the Open Pass, Kiosk Terminal and Pass History pages, plus the CLI history checker.
4. Lagos kiosk pilot
Week 5
Run ServiceSeal at my kiosk in Lagos alongside our paper notebook for regular customers, log real usage on Pudge testnet and note any issues my employee or customers run into.
5. Release & final report
Week 6
Post the pilot transaction hashes, cycle and capacity measurements, demo video and final report on Nervos Talk.
8. Budget ($900 USD)
Area
Hours / Basis
Amount
CKB Type Script, rejection tests and Pudge deployment
24h × $15/hr
$360
CCC transaction builder, CLI verifier and Kiosk Web UI
24h × $15/hr
$360
Two-week Lagos kiosk pilot, demo video and final report
12h × $15/hr
$180
Total
60 hours
$900
Paid in CKB under standard Spark Program rules. I am not asking for hardware, hosting or travel costs since the pilot runs at my own kiosk during normal work hours.
9. How to Verify
Anyone reviewing the project can check the deliverables without relying on a server I control:
Deliverable
How to verify
Type Script & rejection tests
Clone the repo and run the test command to see valid transitions pass and invalid transitions fail in the script.
Deployed Pudge script
Check the published script OutPoint and transaction hashes (opening a pass, valid debits and a rejected overdraw) on the Pudge testnet explorer.
History verifier CLI
Run the CLI checker against any pilot pass ID using a public Pudge RPC URL with the web app turned off, and compare the balance with the explorer.
Kiosk Web UI & pilot
Open the testnet web app, create and debit a test pass and check the pass transaction hashes from the Lagos kiosk pilot in the final report.
10. Ecosystem Value & Post-Spark Plans
We are building ServiceSeal as a reusable CKB primitive for prepaid, terminal-metered state transitions not a one-off app tied to my shop. The 100-byte `SS01` Pass Cell and Type Script give any CKB developer a ready-made primitive for services where a user locks in credit upfront and a terminal or attendant draws it down over time with signed receipts.
For this Spark grant, I am proving the primitive on-chain and piloting it at my own charging kiosk in Lagos where my attendant and customers already deal with notebook disputes. Once the primitive is proven in the kiosk pilot, we plan to use it as the base layer for a broader local utility pass around here because people buy most everyday essentials in retail portions such as buying cooking gas locally by the refill or prepaid water and later pair the primitive with Fiber for payment settlement.

recent_posts.content_text:
1. Project overview Project name: secnev One sentence: secnev is an open, CKB-native risk observatory that turns live cells, scripts, pools and protocol state into explainable risk scores for CKB stablecoins, vaults, xUDT/RGB++ tokens and wallets. Positioning: risk intelligence infrastructure + public dashboard + free API + developer tooling. What already exists: a working MVP on CKB mainnet, 10 assets, real cell-level data, live RUSD/USDI market price and liquidity, iCKB exchange rate/backing, organic holder concentration, wallet exposure, real dCKB transaction replay, alerts, dashboard, API and Vercel deployment. What Spark adds: the two missing halves that turn the MVP into a complete stablecoin risk product: Stable++ protocol state — collateral, oracle and redemption health behind RUSD. Developer Portal v1 — API keys, usage limits, OpenAPI and TypeScript SDK so CKB wallets, DEXs, issuers and data teams can actually integrate secnev. These are one coherent product story: market risk + protocol risk + developer access. Product and funding map flowchart LR A["CKB cells
RPC + Explorer"] --> B["Risk detectors
+ scoring"] S["Stable++ protocol state
collateral / oracle / redemption"] --> B B --> C["Dashboard
+ RUSD detail"] B --> D["Free REST API"] B --> E["Alerts
webhook / Telegram / email"] D --> P["Developer Portal v1
API keys + usage"] P --> K["OpenAPI 3.1
+ TypeScript SDK"] classDef live fill:#0e2a26,stroke:#2dd4a7,color:#e8f0f2,stroke-width:1.5px; classDef spark fill:#2a1a1c,stroke:#ff6b6b,color:#e8f0f2,stroke-width:1.5px; class A,B,C,D,E live; class S,P,K spark; Teal = already live. Coral = Spark-funded delta. Live product screenshots secnev overview1440×1100 94 KB Dashboard: 10 assets, 72/105 live signals, RUSD and USDI critical. RUSD detail1440×1100 91.8 KB RUSD detail: market peg, thin liquidity, organic concentration and evidence. Wallet exposure1440×1100 89.8 KB Wallet exposure: lock label, balance, token holdings and counterparties; taint stays unknown. 2. Team profile Applicant: Tolga Yazan — independent programmar. Role: protocol/data engineering, API design, developer experience and documentation. Background: Writing Rust and Solidity Contracts in EVM and Solana, Smart contract integrations, built the working secnev MVP before this application GitHub: TolgaYazan (TolgaYzn) · GitHub Project repository: GitHub - TolgaYazan/secnev · GitHub Email: tolhoregyachie@gmail.com Discord: @tolhoregyachie Telegram: @tolhoreachie2 3. Project background CKB has real assets but no independent risk layer. The dCKB drain (~24.6M CKB) and the RGB++ forged-proof incident (16.59M CKB, unnoticed for 80 days, per the ckb-adversary proposal) show what the blind spot costs. secnev already answers the market half of the question: 10 CKB assets scored from real mainnet cells. 72/105 signal instances live; 33 explicitly unknown, with coverage disclosure. The readable RUSD/CKB pool is ~26% off peg with ~$1,078 TVL; USDI is ~67% off with ~$165 TVL. Both pools are thin and ~30–40 days stale, and the dashboard publishes that. iCKB exchange rate/backing is live: 1.2989 CKB/iCKB, 2,857,480.70 CKB of Logic DAO deposits against 2,199,999.92 iCKB. Wallet exposure, real dCKB replay, full cell scans, alerts and Vercel deployment are working. Two gaps remain before secnev is a complete RUSD risk product: Protocol solvency is missing. A DEX price can tell a user that RUSD is off peg. It cannot tell them whether the Stable++ vault is solvent, whether the oracle is healthy, or whether redemptions and withdrawals are functioning. Developers cannot onboard. There is no API key, usage limit, OpenAPI contract or SDK. A CKB wallet, DEX, issuer or data team has to reverse-engineer the API and write its own client. 4. Solution Spark funds a focused completion pass on the existing secnev application, not a rebuild, and not a grab bag of new detectors. 4.1 Stable++ protocol-state module Add three protocol-level signals to RUSD, next to the existing market signals: Collateral health — vault cells, total debt, collateral ratio, MCR/TCR/CCR, liquidation buffer. Oracle health — oracle cell age, feed/publisher identity, deviation from the live DEX price. Redemption / withdrawal state — redemption fee/base rate, pause state, and whether the protocol can honour exits. Every field is sourced from on-chain data. If a field is not publicly accessible or cannot be verified, it stays unknown with the reason published. Nothing is invented. 4.2 Developer Portal v1 Add a /developers onboarding layer on top of the existing API: self-serve hashed API keys with revocation; free-tier usage limits and rate limits; OpenAPI 3.1 contract; TypeScript SDK with typed methods; copy-paste curl/TypeScript/Python examples; usage panel. This turns secnev from “a good dashboard” into infrastructure other CKB teams can build on. 4.3 Validation Run 10 validation sessions with a mix of CKB depositors, wallet engineers, DEX/issuer teams and data analysts. The output is a public report: did the protocol signals change a decision, and did a developer get to a first successful request in under ten minutes? 4.4 Extensible for the next CKB protocol or token This is not a one-off RUSD integration. The Spark work will formalize the pattern already used by secnev: asset/token registry — add a new xUDT/RGB++ token by type hash and metadata; protocol adapter — implement getState() for a new stablecoin or vault and map it to signals; pool/vault descriptors — add a new UTXOSwap pool or vault through configuration; API and portal — new entities appear through the registry and OpenAPI, not hand-written endpoints. The Stable++ adapter is the reference implementation. Adding the next CKB mainnet protocol should be a bounded adapter + config change, not a rewrite of ingestion, scoring, API or dashboard. Explicitly out of scope no new assets or new risk categories beyond the Stable++ state; no paid tiers or billing; no MCP or x402 in this round; no sanctions/taint or transaction monitoring; no issuer-controlled ranking, token or paid scores. 5. Technical approach Stack: Node.js 24 + TypeScript, native node:sqlite, CKB public RPC get_cells, CKB Explorer API, vanilla JS dashboard, Vercel static + serverless functions, Upstash Redis free tier for API keys/usage. Architecture: Stable++ vault/oracle cells ─┐ UTXOSwap RUSD pool ──────────┼─> detectors ─> score ─> API / dashboard CKB RPC / Explorer ──────────┘ │ ├─ webhook / Telegram / email └─ /developers portal │ keys + usage (Redis) Stable++ adapter: locate vault/debt/oracle/redemption cells from deployed scripts; decode cell data with the existing little-endian/u128 and script-fingerprint utilities; add collateral_health, oracle_health and redemption_state to the vault detector set; cross-check oracle price against the live RUSD/CKB pool, publishing both plus TVL and last-trade age; fixtures and tests so the adapter is reviewable without a live wallet. The adapter sits behind a small ProtocolAdapter interface. Asset metadata, pools and vaults stay registry/config-driven, so the next CKB protocol or token is an additive adapter + config change rather than a new fork of the ingestion, scoring, API or dashboard. Developer Portal: keys are sk_live_; only SHA-256 hashes are stored; x-api-key header; anonymous requests are allowed but IP-limited; rate limits use Redis INCR + TTL windows; portal endpoints consolidated into one /api/portal function; the unused Vercel /history route is retired to stay within Hobby’s 12-function limit (history remains in the local API); one openapi.json is the source of truth for docs and the SDK; the SDK is a thin typed fetch wrapper with no runtime dependencies. Fail-closed rule: missing or stale protocol data is unknown, never “safe”. Coverage and confidence remain visible in every response. 6. To-do list Week Work Milestone 1 Map Stable++ vault/debt/oracle/redemption scripts and cell layouts; document every field and every unknown; create fixtures Protocol map + fixture set 2 Implement the Stable++ adapter; add the three signals and unit tests Adapter merged; tests pass 3 Integrate the new signals into the dashboard and API; deploy a preview with evidence/coverage labels Public preview with RUSD protocol state 4 Build Developer Portal v1: /developers, hashed keys, usage/rate limits, OpenAPI, TypeScript SDK Portal + SDK live on preview 5 Run 10 validation sessions (CKB depositors, wallet/DEX/issuer/data teams); fix the highest-impact onboarding and signal issues Validation notes + issue list 6 Final docs, security pass, public validation report, completion report, handover Spark completion package Every week ends with a verifiable artifact. 7. Required funding and breakdown Requested: $1,000 USD equivalent, 100% in CKB. CKB amount will be calculated at the Committee’s approval-day rate. The request is denominated in USD so the scope is stable. Item Amount Purpose Stable++ protocol-state adapter $250 Cell/oracle mapping, three signals, fixtures, tests Developer Portal v1 $350 API keys, usage/rate limits, OpenAPI, TypeScript SDK, portal UI Dashboard/API integration $100 Wire protocol signals and portal into the existing app 10 validation sessions $100 User and developer recruitment, sessions, synthesis, report Documentation $150 User and Developer Guides Infrastructure $50 Vercel + Upstash Redis free-tier overage / monitoring | Total | $1,000 | 100% CKB | 8. Deliverables and how to verify Deliverables Stable++ adapter with fixtures. Three live RUSD protocol signals: collateral health, oracle health, redemption/withdrawal state. Dashboard + API integration with evidence, confidence and coverage. /developers portal with quickstart, API reference and examples. Self-serve hashed API keys with revocation. Usage/rate limits and quota panel. OpenAPI 3.1 contract and TypeScript SDK. Tests for the adapter, key hashing, auth, quota and revocation. 10-session validation report and public completion report. How to verify (no code review required) Open https://secnev.vercel.app, open RUSD, and inspect the three protocol signals and their evidence. Call GET /api/v1/assets/{RUSD-id} and check the JSON signals. Open https://secnev.vercel.app/developers, create a key, run the displayed curl command, see usage increase, then revoke the key and confirm 401. Run the SDK example; it returns typed asset data. 1. Project overview

Project name: secnev

One sentence: secnev is an open, CKB-native risk observatory that turns live cells, scripts, pools and protocol state into explainable risk scores for CKB stablecoins, vaults, xUDT/RGB++ tokens and wallets.

Positioning: risk intelligence infrastructure + public dashboard + free API + developer tooling.

What already exists: a working MVP on CKB mainnet, 10 assets, real cell-level data, live RUSD/USDI market price and liquidity, iCKB exchange rate/backing, organic holder concentration, wallet exposure, real dCKB transaction replay, alerts, dashboard, API and Vercel deployment.

What Spark adds: the two missing halves that turn the MVP into a complete stablecoin risk product:

  1. Stable++ protocol state — collateral, oracle and redemption health behind RUSD.
  2. Developer Portal v1 — API keys, usage limits, OpenAPI and TypeScript SDK so CKB wallets, DEXs, issuers and data teams can actually integrate secnev.

These are one coherent product story: market risk + protocol risk + developer access.

Product and funding map

    A["CKB cells<br/>RPC + Explorer"] --> B["Risk detectors<br/>+ scoring"]
    S["Stable++ protocol state<br/>collateral / oracle / redemption"] --> B
    B --> C["Dashboard<br/>+ RUSD detail"]
    B --> D["Free REST API"]

Live product screenshots

Dashboard: 10 assets, 72/105 live signals, RUSD and USDI critical.

RUSD detail1440×1100 91.8 KB

RUSD detail: market peg, thin liquidity, organic concentration and evidence.

Wallet exposure: lock label, balance, token holdings and counterparties; taint stays unknown.

2. Team profile

Applicant: Tolga Yazan — independent programmar.

Role: protocol/data engineering, API design, developer experience and documentation.

Background: Writing Rust and Solidity Contracts in EVM and Solana, Smart contract integrations, built the working secnev MVP before this application

GitHub: TolgaYazan (TolgaYzn) · GitHub

Project repository: GitHub - TolgaYazan/secnev · GitHub

Email: tolhoregyachie@gmail.com

Discord: @tolhoregyachie

Telegram: @tolhoreachie2

3. Project background

CKB has real assets but no independent risk layer. The dCKB drain (~24.6M CKB) and the RGB++ forged-proof incident (16.59M CKB, unnoticed for 80 days, per the ckb-adversary proposal) show what the blind spot costs.

secnev already answers the market half of the question:

  • 10 CKB assets scored from real mainnet cells.
  • 72/105 signal instances live; 33 explicitly unknown, with coverage disclosure.
  • The readable RUSD/CKB pool is ~26% off peg with ~$1,078 TVL; USDI is ~67% off with ~$165 TVL. Both pools are thin and ~30–40 days stale, and the dashboard publishes that.
  • iCKB exchange rate/backing is live: 1.2989 CKB/iCKB, 2,857,480.70 CKB of Logic DAO deposits against 2,199,999.92 iCKB.
  • Wallet exposure, real dCKB replay, full cell scans, alerts and Vercel deployment are working.

Two gaps remain before secnev is a complete RUSD risk product:

  1. Protocol solvency is missing. A DEX price can tell a user that RUSD is off peg. It cannot tell them whether the Stable++ vault is solvent, whether the oracle is healthy, or whether redemptions and withdrawals are functioning.
  2. Developers cannot onboard. There is no API key, usage limit, OpenAPI contract or SDK. A CKB wallet, DEX, issuer or data team has to reverse-engineer the API and write its own client.

4. Solution

Spark funds a focused completion pass on the existing secnev application, not a rebuild, and not a grab bag of new detectors.

4.1 Stable++ protocol-state module

Add three protocol-level signals to RUSD, next to the existing market signals:

  1. Collateral health — vault cells, total debt, collateral ratio, MCR/TCR/CCR, liquidation buffer.
  2. Oracle health — oracle cell age, feed/publisher identity, deviation from the live DEX price.
  3. Redemption / withdrawal state — redemption fee/base rate, pause state, and whether the protocol can honour exits.

Every field is sourced from on-chain data. If a field is not publicly accessible or cannot be verified, it stays unknown with the reason published. Nothing is invented.

4.2 Developer Portal v1

Add a /developers onboarding layer on top of the existing API:

  • self-serve hashed API keys with revocation;
  • free-tier usage limits and rate limits;
  • OpenAPI 3.1 contract;
  • TypeScript SDK with typed methods;
  • copy-paste curl/TypeScript/Python examples;
  • usage panel.

This turns secnev from “a good dashboard” into infrastructure other CKB teams can build on.

4.3 Validation

Run 10 validation sessions with a mix of CKB depositors, wallet engineers, DEX/issuer teams and data analysts. The output is a public report: did the protocol signals change a decision, and did a developer get to a first successful request in under ten minutes?

4.4 Extensible for the next CKB protocol or token

This is not a one-off RUSD integration. The Spark work will formalize the pattern already used by secnev:

  • asset/token registry — add a new xUDT/RGB++ token by type hash and metadata;
  • protocol adapter — implement getState() for a new stablecoin or vault and map it to signals;
  • pool/vault descriptors — add a new UTXOSwap pool or vault through configuration;
  • API and portal — new entities appear through the registry and OpenAPI, not hand-written endpoints.

The Stable++ adapter is the reference implementation. Adding the next CKB mainnet protocol should be a bounded adapter + config change, not a rewrite of ingestion, scoring, API or dashboard.

Explicitly out of scope

  • no new assets or new risk categories beyond the Stable++ state;
  • no paid tiers or billing;
  • no MCP or x402 in this round;
  • no sanctions/taint or transaction monitoring;
  • no issuer-controlled ranking, token or paid scores.

5. Technical approach

Stack: Node.js 24 + TypeScript, native node:sqlite, CKB public RPC get_cells, CKB Explorer API, vanilla JS dashboard, Vercel static + serverless functions, Upstash Redis free tier for API keys/usage.

Architecture:

Stable++ vault/oracle cells ─┐
UTXOSwap RUSD pool ──────────┼─> detectors ─> score ─> API / dashboard
CKB RPC / Explorer ──────────┘                         │
                                                       ├─ webhook / Telegram / email
                                                       └─ /developers portal
                                                              │
                                                     keys + usage (Redis)

Stable++ adapter:

  • locate vault/debt/oracle/redemption cells from deployed scripts;
  • decode cell data with the existing little-endian/u128 and script-fingerprint utilities;
  • add collateral_health, oracle_health and redemption_state to the vault detector set;
  • cross-check oracle price against the live RUSD/CKB pool, publishing both plus TVL and last-trade age;
  • fixtures and tests so the adapter is reviewable without a live wallet.

The adapter sits behind a small ProtocolAdapter interface. Asset metadata, pools and vaults stay registry/config-driven, so the next CKB protocol or token is an additive adapter + config change rather than a new fork of the ingestion, scoring, API or dashboard.

Developer Portal:

  • keys are sk_live_<random>; only SHA-256 hashes are stored;
  • x-api-key header; anonymous requests are allowed but IP-limited;
  • rate limits use Redis INCR + TTL windows;
  • portal endpoints consolidated into one /api/portal function; the unused Vercel /history route is retired to stay within Hobby’s 12-function limit (history remains in the local API);
  • one openapi.json is the source of truth for docs and the SDK;
  • the SDK is a thin typed fetch wrapper with no runtime dependencies.

Fail-closed rule: missing or stale protocol data is unknown, never “safe”. Coverage and confidence remain visible in every response.

  1. Stable++ adapter with fixtures.

recent_posts.author: Steven_Hert
recent_posts.content_text:
Update: ckbup now installs five tools.
The second step is merged. ckbup install now covers ckb, fnn and ckb-light-client as well as ckb-debugger and ckb-cli.
cargo install --git https://github.com/steven3002/ckbup
ckbup install ckb
ckbup install fnn
ckbup install ckb-light-client
What changed:
The right build for your machine. Each project names its release files differently, and ckbup reads each scheme. For fnn and ckb-light-client it prefers the portable builds: their standard Linux builds need glibc 2.39 and 2.38, while the portable ones run on glibc 2.34. --portable asks for the portable build where a project publishes one. ckb’s release notes recommend it if you see “illegal instruction” errors. CentOS builds are skipped, since upstream plans to stop shipping them.
Whole release packages. Config folders and docs stay next to the binary, and companion tools such as fnn-cli go on your PATH too. The copy of ckb-cli bundled inside the ckb release is left off PATH, because ckbup manages ckb-cli as its own tool.
Checksums, or a clear stop. Every download is checked against the SHA-256 that GitHub publishes for the release file. Releases published before mid-2025 usually have no checksum at all, so ckbup refuses them unless you pass --allow-unverified:
$ ckbup install ckb-light-client@v0.4.1
error: GitHub lists no SHA-256 for ckb-light-client_v0.4.1-x86_64-windows.tar.gz, and ckb-light-client
publishes no checksum file for v0.4.1; older releases often have none. Re-run with --allow-unverified
to install it without verification
It also picked up Fiber’s fnn v0.10.1, released this week, as soon as it appeared.
On Windows, ckb-light-client needs the Microsoft Visual C++ runtime; the README says so.
Next: list, use and remove, so you can see what’s installed and switch between versions.
If you run fnn or the light client on an older Linux, I’d like to hear whether the portable builds work for you.

CKB IDL — Milestone 0 Foundation Report
Status: Draft for publication. Foundation deliverables are available for review;
final close-out items are listed below.
Milestone 0 establishes the development and delivery foundation for the CKB Script
Registry and the broader CKB IDL lifecycle. The registry repository, public roadmap,
confirmed ecosystem release plan, local development environment, CI, contribution
and security policies, and MIT license are now published.
This milestone builds on the existing IDL 0.1.0 specification and released Rust
crates. Those earlier releases are the baseline, not newly delivered M0 work.
Project proposal
Public roadmap and issue board
Registry repository
Implementation baseline: b37ef14
Passing CI for that commit
M0 deliverables and evidence
Promised deliverable
Delivered work
Review evidence
Public roadmap and issue board
Public organization project with 24 issues grouped into M0–M4 repository milestones. Issues include outcomes, acceptance criteria, and dependencies.
Project board, milestones
Confirmed release plan
Maintainer-approved ecosystem plan covering existing releases, component ownership, compatibility, cross-repository sequencing, and independent package release decisions.
RELEASE_PLAN.md
Registry repository scaffold
Rust/Axum server with tracing, a health endpoint, configurable binding, graceful shutdown, and a local filesystem object store.
Server source, manifest
CI and local Docker Compose environment
Formatting, locked tests/build, Compose validation, PostgreSQL Alpine with readiness/persistence, and an optional API container build.
CI workflow, Compose, Dockerfile, setup guide
Contribution/security documentation
Development and PR guidance, branch promotion rules, current security boundaries, and vulnerability-reporting instructions. MIT licensing is also included.
Contribution guide, security policy, MIT license
Development setup and implementation decisions
The default local setup runs the API directly with Cargo and starts only
PostgreSQL 17 Alpine through Docker Compose. Artifact storage uses the Rust
object_store local filesystem backend at .local/object-storage/; it needs
no separate object-storage server, bucket, or cloud credentials.
An initial MinIO approach was replaced with this simpler setup. MinIO, its Go
source build, and the AWS CLI initialization container are not required. The
object-store abstraction leaves room for a hosted backend later without adding
cloud-provider dependencies now.
The optional multi-stage API Docker build produced a 78.3 MB runtime image.
The PostgreSQL Alpine image measured 297.2 MB, for approximately 375.5 MB
combined image size. These are recorded image sizes, not a bound on temporary
build storage, compiler caches, or persistent data.
New feature/fix work follows separate branches into dev, then batch validation
on staging, followed by promotion to master. The maintainer authorized the
remaining M0 foundation/documentation work directly on dev. The evidence in
this report is published on dev; it has not yet been promoted through staging
to master.
Testing and validation
The linked GitHub Actions run passed for commit b37ef14:
Rust formatting check.
cargo test --locked.
cargo build --locked.
Docker Compose configuration validation.
The two automated storage tests verify that an object can be written and read
when the store is reopened, and that a file cannot be used as the storage root.
Test source.
Additional local checks during M0 verified API health responses, storage-folder
initialization, graceful SIGTERM shutdown, PostgreSQL readiness, and database
persistence across container recreation. The optional API image was built,
started, passed its container/HTTP health checks, and exited cleanly after stop.
These were engineering checks, not additional jobs in the linked CI run.
No external security audit, hosted registry acceptance test, or new on-chain
verification demonstration is claimed for M0.
Reproducing the foundation checks
Requirements: Rust stable, Docker, and Docker Compose v2.
git clone --branch dev https://github.com/ckb-idl/script-registry.git
cd script-registry
git checkout b37ef146f897d1b78a633bd16df0536a5a978ad6
cargo fmt --manifest-path server/Cargo.toml --all -- --check
cargo test --manifest-path server/Cargo.toml --locked
cargo build --manifest-path server/Cargo.toml --locked
docker compose config --quiet
docker compose up -d --wait
cargo run --manifest-path server/Cargo.toml --locked
In another terminal, request http://localhost:3000/health:
curl --fail http://localhost:3000/health
The expected response is {"status":"ok"}. The server creates the local object
storage directory automatically. Environment overrides are documented in the
README; an .env file is optional for the current local defaults.
Stop the API with Ctrl-C, then run docker compose down from the repository root.
Do not add --volumes unless intentionally deleting the development database.
Current limitations and close-out
The API is a development scaffold. Publisher authentication, namespaces, release
publication, immutable content-addressed artifact handling, database integration,
search, and chain verification remain future milestone work. /health reports
process health only.
GitHub private vulnerability reporting is still disabled. The published security
policy states that limitation and provides a contact-request fallback without
asking reporters to disclose vulnerability details publicly. A confidential
reporting channel must be enabled or confirmed to finish the remaining security
reporting-channel acceptance item.
CI currently triggers on pushes and pull requests for dev and master;
staging is not included yet. Staging batches require explicit validation until
that configuration is extended.
The release-plan and policy issues should be reconciled with their published
evidence and remaining acceptance criteria. This report still needs publication
in the proposal thread; the reporting issue must not be treated as complete
merely because this draft exists. Community acceptance and any funding action
are separate from publishing the implementation.
Next milestone
M1 focuses on the registry publication core: the PostgreSQL package/release model,
immutable artifact storage, GitHub OAuth publisher authentication, namespace and
release publication, and public read APIs. Scripts without IDL artifacts remain
eligible for registration.
The public board coordinates ecosystem work. Implementation issues can move to
their owning repositories as client, derive/exporter, specification, TypeScript,
and Molecule work proceeds; those components are not all implemented in the
registry repository.
Community review
Reviewers can inspect the pinned sources, reproduce the local checks, and compare
the delivered foundation with the M0 proposal scope. Feedback on the development
workflow, release coordination, storage approach, and reporting evidence is
welcome through the proposal thread or
repository issues.

Project name: TITANHOLD CKB Pay

Type: payment / checkout integration (library + small demo service), not a new L1, not a token, not a live production rail.
2. Team Profile
Core member: Hennadii Kovalenko (Gena) — solo technical founder, builder and applicant.
Background: Self-taught programmer since 2004. Solo founder of TITANHOLD LLC (Wyoming, USA; organized 14 October 2026). Builds a studio and platform for small businesses: websites, bots, and AI agents. Amanda is the platform’s AI assistant: she takes the order, issues a written quote, and the platform builds the work. Clients can see a demo on their own data before they pay.
CKB experience: I do not claim prior shipped CKB production software. This proposal is a planned prototype, which is why a public repo and a short, verifiable testnet demo are the right Spark scope.

Site: https://titanhold.app

Nervos Talk: hennadii

That matters to the CKB ecosystem if the checkout is real and small: a business that already has paying customers should be able to offer a CKB payment option without pretending the integration already exists. Spark is the right size of grant for a 6-week testnet prototype, not for a production payments product.
4. Solution
Build a narrow, open-source checkout module:
An order (created through Amanda or the Telegram bot) gets a unique payment request.
The payer connects a supported CKB wallet and pays the requested amount on CKB testnet first.
The module verifies the payment and only then marks that order as paid.
A reviewer can run the demo, see the status change, and check a testnet explorer link, without having to audit every line of code.

I will not claim this is live, that it is already wired into production titanhold.app, or that clients can already pay in CKB.

Tooling (planned, official first): CCC (CKB JavaScript SDK) and a supported wallet such as JoyID, on CKB testnet. If a planned tool is a poor fit once work starts, the weekly update will say so and name the replacement. I will not invent APIs or unofficial shortcuts in this draft.
Architecture (planned):
order — a minimal order record (id, amount, currency/unit, status).
payment request — binds one order to one CKB payment intent.
wallet connect — testnet wallet session for the payer.
verify — confirm the payment against the request before flipping status to paid.
adapters — a small interface the Amanda/web checkout and the Telegram-bot path can call. The grant delivers the interface and a demo hook, not a claim that production titanhold.app already uses it.
Hard points: tying a payment unambiguously to one order; verifying payment without a human staring at raw transactions; keeping secrets (keys, mnemonics, .env) out of the public repo; making verification cheap for reviewers (script + testnet explorer, not a full code review).
What will not be in the repo: private keys, mnemonics, production credentials, or any invitation to send mainnet funds.

Six weeks, one person.

Week 2. Scaffold the repo so a reviewer can install and run a stub. Implement testnet wallet connect and a payment request for a dummy order.

Week 5. Adapter for a Telegram-bot payment link (same payment request, different surface).

A. Deliverables
Public GitHub repository (MIT): GitHub - wolkodaww123-ctrl/titanhold-ckb-pay: TITANHOLD CKB Pay: work-in-progress prototype of CKB payments for small-business orders (MIT) · GitHub — design, source for the prototype, and documentation. Adapters — documented interfaces for the Amanda/web path and the Telegram-bot path, with a demo hook for each. Done when those interfaces exist in the repo and are described; not done by claiming production titanhold.app already charges CKB.
Completion note — what was planned, what shipped, what changed, and a funding-use summary versus this breakdown.
B. How to verify (without a heavy code review)
Clone the public repo and follow the README on CKB testnet (no mainnet funds).
Run the stated commands / tests.
Create a dummy order, complete a testnet payment, and confirm the status change.
Open the testnet explorer link produced by the demo and check it matches the order’s payment request.
Read the short verification notes and the completion note.
Environment: a current Node.js toolchain (version pinned in the repo when implementation starts), a CKB testnet wallet with test tokens, and internet access. No paid third-party API key should be required for the basic demo.
Cost of review: a single pass through the README and one testnet payment, not a line-by-line audit.
9. Current State vs. Funded Work
Current state: TITANHOLD the studio is operating and has paying clients. There is no CKB payment integration today. The Spark repository is a planned-prototype README and license (public on GitHub now). There is no testnet demo yet.
Funded work (the difference): the six-week plan above — design, testnet checkout, verification, two adapters, documentation, and a completion note.
These two lists are not the same. Client revenue and the live website are not evidence that CKB checkout already exists.
10. CKB Alignment
This project uses CKB as the settlement network for a real checkout path, starting on testnet. The first implementation plan is to use official CKB tooling (CCC and a supported wallet such as JoyID) rather than a side-system that only mentions CKB in passing.
I am not claiming a deep new use of the Cell Model, Spore/DOB, or Fiber in this first six-week slice. If Fiber or another CKB-native rail is clearly a better fit once Week 1 research is done, I will say so in the public repo and in the weekly sync, and keep the scope to a finishable prototype. If the work stays on a straightforward CCC + wallet checkout, that is still a direct CKB payment integration for an existing order-taking product, not a generic tool with a CKB logo attached.

Legal: TITANHOLD LLC, Wyoming, USA, organized 14 October 2026.

Update. Twine works with Fiber Studio and Cellula Wallet.
Fiber Studio is the desktop app. It runs the official Fiber node on your computer. Cellula Wallet is the other one, in the browser and on Android. It pays over Fiber, and you do not run a node for it.
The trade is the same.
The buyer makes a Fiber invoice in Fiber Studio or Cellula Wallet and pastes it into Twine. The secret stays in that wallet.
The seller pays the hold invoice from their own copy of either wallet. After that, the coins cannot be pulled back early.
On release, Twine pays the buyer’s invoice. The CKB arrives in the wallet that made it.
The local money still goes from one account to the other. Twine does not hold it, and Twine does not hold a key that can spend the locked CKB.
Fiber Studio: https://www.getfiberstudio.com/
Cellula Wallet is on testnet, for web and Android.
